📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

For the fourth year in a row, Formula 1 took over Las Vegas, transforming the Strip into a three-day collision of sport, nightlife, celebrity culture, and over-the-top entertainment.

The 2026 Formula 1 Heineken Las Vegas Grand Prix arrived at the end of a banner season for the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team. Kimi Antonelli had already made history as Formula 1’s youngest-ever World Champion at 20 years old, while Mercedes secured its first Constructors’ Championship since 2021.

But two days before Antonelli and teammate George Russell raced through the streets of Las Vegas, they were competing in very different vehicles.

According to recent reports, organized by Marriott Bonvoy with Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, the Fountains of Bellagio were transformed into a Formula 1-inspired racecourse, where the drivers and five Marriott Bonvoy members raced custom speedboats across the hotel’s famed waters. The event was part of Marriott Bonvoy Moments, which offers members access to exclusive experiences through the travel program’s longtime partners, including Mercedes (Marriott Bonvoy members can also currently bid on packages to see Celine Dion in Paris).

Russell looked comfortable behind the wheel, smoothly maneuvering around the course, while Antonelli took a more chaotic approach, colliding with buoys, stalling his boat, and taking a few unexpected detours. The professional drivers ultimately lost to two Bonvoy members, who posted the fastest average time.

Afterward, Antonelli and Russell headed to the Mercedes Fan Hub on Bellagio Drive, where they tested their pit-stop skills and greeted fans. Across the Strip, Williams driver Carlos Sainz returned to ARIA Resort & Casino with his Smooth Operator Dance Lounge, while Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc met fans at Bellagio’s Ferrari boutique.

Formula 1’s growing popularity has increasingly turned Grand Prix weekends into multi-day cultural events, and Las Vegas pushes that formula to its extreme.

Sources indicate that on Friday night, the spectacle shifted from racing to rodeo. Uber and Zoox transformed MGM Grand Garden Arena into an invitation-only “Disco Rodeo” celebrating Zoox’s autonomous robotaxis joining the Uber app. Guests entered a surreal Western-meets-disco setting filled with mirrored decor before professional bull riders, trick riders, and roping performers took over a dirt arena.

In a recent development, close to midnight, Grammy-winning artist Kacey Musgraves rode into the arena on horseback before performing for a crowd that included Teyana Taylor and Tiësto. Musgraves moved through songs including “Dry Spell” and “Butterflies,” turning one of Las Vegas’ biggest arenas into an unlikely combination of concert, nightclub, and rodeo.

Sources indicate that by race day, the action returned to the Strip, where the paddock hosted a steady stream of A-list guests. Anthony Mackie, Keanu Reeves, Damson Idris, Simu Liu, and Kim Kardashian were among the famous faces spotted around the circuit, while K-pop artist REI AMI headlined the pre-race Grid Gigs.

Before Jordin Sparks sang the national anthem, 11 celebrity guests took over for the traditional drivers’ parade, navigating the 6.2-kilometer circuit in drivable Lego Formula 1 cars made from more than 28,000 bricks each. DJ Carl Cox represented Mercedes, Lisa drove for Ferrari, Gordon Ramsay took McLaren’s wheel and Terry Crews represented Cadillac. Australian DJ Fisher, driving for Red Bull, took the win.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit itself is built for spectacle, threading 17 corners through the heart of the city and past some of its most recognizable landmarks. By Saturday night, grandstands, hotel terraces and hospitality suites were packed with fans watching Formula 1 cars flash beneath the neon lights, with the Sphere glowing over the circuit and the Strip providing a backdrop unlike any other race on the calendar.

When the lights went out, the 50-lap Las Vegas Grand Prix delivered the fast-paced drama the city had promised. Max Verstappen and George Russell repeatedly battled near the front, while Ferrari teammates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc made contact late in the race. Mercedes’ hopes of a podium faded in the closing laps, with Antonelli finishing fourth and Russell ninth.

Verstappen ultimately claimed his third Las Vegas victory, crossing the line ahead of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who completed the podium. Actor Chris Pratt waved the checkered flag as the four-time World Champion crossed the finish line.

Official F1 Vegas merch is still available online and on sale right now for Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that the end of the race did little to slow Las Vegas down. The Backstreet Boys headlined Formula 1’s inaugural official afterparty at Sphere, carrying the celebration late into the night. The afterparty matched the city around it: energetic, entertaining and intentionally excessive, keeping the momentum going long after the final cars left the circuit.

Las Vegas marked the first stop in Formula 1’s final triple-header of 2026. Next, the grid heads to the Qatar Grand Prix before closing the season at the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, bringing another year of racing and the spectacle surrounding it to a close.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Black Friday deals have arrived, and although it's only Tuesday, there are already plenty of great discounts on the best action cameras, 360 cameras and vlogging cameras.

Industry observers note that I'm Pete, reviews editor here at Tom's Guide and the man in charge of our camera coverage. I test all action and 360 cameras, so I have to keep an eye on pricing throughout the year. This is usually the best time of the year to pick up a deal on action cameras and other gear. After all, it's never too early to start planning out your content for next year!

In a recent development, my favorite deal so far is on, well, my favorite action camera. The DJI Osmo Action 6 is the best action camera around, and is now $70 off at Amazon. This is the latest DJI flagship, so it's the first time I've seen this camera discounted in the U.S., and $70 is nothing to sniff at.

The biggest discount, and arguably best deal around right now, is on the GoPro MAX2 360 camera, which is down 45% from its $499 MSRP to just $274 at Amazon. Crazy value, in all honesty. But there's plenty more where that came from, including vlogging cameras like the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 at its lowest ever U.S. price of $373 at Amazon.

I'm only including deals that are actually good. I'm discounting any products (ahem, Insta360 X3, ahem) whose prices have been deliberately hiked before the sales events to make it look like a good deal. Read on for genuinely good savings!

Industry observers note that don't be fooled by the $299 MSRP — this camera usually sits around the $220. However, at $179, the DJI Osmo Action 4 still just hit its lowest price in the U.S., so there's never been a better time to pick up this little camera. It might be a couple of years old, but if you need professional-looking 4K video for YouTube, it's still plenty capable enough.

Industry observers note that I'm shocked at this one. The GoPro MAX2 is the latest 360 camera from GoPro and a serious contender against the Insta360 X5 and X6, and Osmo 360 II. The fact it's second place in price order on this list is therefore pretty wild. If you want the flexibility of 8K 360 footage, I'm pretty sure this deal right here is the cheapest way there's ever been to get that.

Recent findings suggest that the X4 Air is the revamped X4 — the first 8K 360 camera. The X4 Air packs some choice updates, namely to its audio (featuring the X5's wind guard) and stripped down weight. It's dropped to $299 before, but never lower, and tends to sit at the $399 MSRP outside of sales events. This is already a good deal, but I'd maybe wait to see if it drops a little further as Black Friday itself approaches.

DJI has faced an uphill struggle in the U.S. recently, thanks to its ongoing feud with the government and trade tariffs affecting its pricing. As such, the newer Pocket 4 models are borderline outrageously priced in the U.S. The DJI Osmo Pocket 3 is still a brilliant choice for content creators though, offering 4K gimbal-stabilized video. This is actually the lowest we've seen it drop (the previous low being $378).

Sources indicate that the DJI Osmo Action 6 is the latest and greatest flagship action camera. It's my top pick for action cameras generally, and it's the camera I use personally. It offers the best blend of high-res capture, stabilization, battery life and waterproofing. As this camera is still relatively new, this is the first time we've seen a serious discount in the U.S., and $70 is a decent saving for the best-of-the-best, if you ask me.

Industry observers note that I gave the Insta360 X5 our full five stars when I reviewed it in 2025. And it was well deserved. At the time, it was pushing the boundaries of what a 360 camera could do, with 8K/30fps 360 footage, strong internal audio and effective wind reduction. Insta360 gear always has a premium, but this is the lowest price we've seen the X5 drop yet.

Not satisfied with DJI constantly wearing the 'content creator gimbal camera' crown, Insta360 has had a pop. The Luna Pro offers 8K HDR gimbal-stabilized footage, giving you effortlessly smooth, professional output and plenty of space to crop while maintaining 4K resolution. It's pricey, but since when has cutting edge camera gear been cheap? Again, this is a pretty latest camera, so this is the first time we're seeing real sizeable discounts.

In a recent development, the GoPro Mission 1 Pro is still fairly fresh, so typically sits around $699, but it's spent a couple of months at $599 recently. So while this is a good deal, it could well drop further as we approach the weekend. Keep an eye out. The Mission 1 Pro is an awesome camera for pros, offering 8K open gate and custom firmware via GoPro Labs.

It has been revealed that the Insta360 X6 is the latest flagship 360 camera from Insta360. It offers improved imaging over the X5, excellent battery life, an OLED display, and is the first Insta360 camera to feature internal storage. This isn't a huge discount, which is to be expected given how fresh this camera is, but it's still the lowest price we've yet seen the X6 drop.

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • Sources indicate that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

Sources indicate that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Sources indicate that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

It has been revealed that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

Sources indicate that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly indicates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

According to recent reports, he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs reveals the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

Industry observers note that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very rapidly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

In a recent development, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Recent findings suggest that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

According to recent reports, the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” notes Habbal.

Sources indicate that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Sources indicate that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

Sources indicate that the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

It has been revealed that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller states with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” claims Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

Recent findings suggest that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

According to recent reports, twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

In a recent development, among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Sources indicate that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Sources indicate that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller notes with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

It has been revealed that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

According to recent reports, “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” notes Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Recent findings suggest that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

It has been revealed that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller claims.

According to recent reports, who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

As the 2026 F1 season made its final U.S. stop of the year, Las Vegas once again turned its neon-lit streets into an impressive, 17-turn race that wound its way through The Strip, with drivers whizzing past the city’s most iconic landmarks. On Sunday, Max Verstappen took home the checkered flag at the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix after a nail-biting finish, with McLaren’s Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri posting a double-podium finish to complete the top three.

With F1’s growing prominence in the U.S., new fans continue to enter the high-speed world of racing. But while the rules of Formula 1 seem simple enough — the first car to pass the checkered flag after 50-odd laps, wins — it does take some time to truly understand the complexities of the sport.

Rolling Stone sat down with McLaren drivers Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix to glean some tips on how new fans can optimize their viewing experience.

Industry observers note that norris advises the audience to watch onboard videos and listen to the commentators who make the race more understandable. “When you then see the onboard cameras in the driver’s eye [line], I think it looks a lot more realistic [since] that is what I’m seeing with my head,” he says, “So I think that gives a much better experience. The more that they can do that, and get the sensation of speed, the easier it will be for people to understand.”.

And while new viewers might only focus on the leaderboard, Piastri begs to differ. “I think the first thing about Formula 1 is not everyone’s car is the same, so I think just because some people aren’t winning, it doesn’t necessarily mean that they’re worse than the people that are winning,” he says. “Oftentimes the racing in the midfield can sometimes be more entertaining than the racing at the front.”.

The drivers both say that strategy shifts within varying climate conditions, tire compounds and their impact to performance and longevity, and the car’s on-track behavior are just a few of the factors being considered on the sidelines during every race.

Sources indicate that as part of their preparation, the team reviews prior races of the current season, as well as footage of the same track last year to see any learnings that could apply. Norris emphasizes how the addition of new cameras showing extra angles on the track can help the driver’s pre-race POV while adding to the immersive fan experience.

T-Mobile, F1’s regional 5G innovation partner, supports this by (literally) taking connectivity to latest heights, with more than 20 5G-connected cameras that supply additional angles and track views. With its partnership with Apple TV, more angles are made available to the customer, in addition to a private 5G network to ensure reliable connectivity for broadcast feeds.

“We saw an opportunity with the technology-forward nature of the sport to be able to come in and look at how could we provide network solutions that are actually making the experience better,” offers Amy Azzi, VP of Sponsorships and Events at T-Mobile.

Azzi highlights the “additional broadcast views and angles, using our connectivity, and devices that are able to capture those angles and bring them into a more functional broadcast or into the app, which allow more opportunities for fans to engage.”.

Sources indicate that for fans who can’t watch the races live, the network giant recently introduced T-Mix, where customers can mix and match benefits and entertainment options every three months, including streamers like Apple TV, home of the F1 U.S. broadcast, alongside other premier streamers, travel partners, and music providers.

At the end of the day, the McLaren duo’s most important connections are to their supporters. Piastri says he’s collected his fair share of fan gifts this year, shouting out a glitter-covered cowboy hat in his helmet design, to a hardcover book with special fan messages. “Hearing some some people’s stories and how coming to an F1 race is literally their life dream, and being able to to help them kind of fulfill that dream is is really cool,” he says.

Norris emphasizes that fans are the most notable thing in their sport. To wit: the driver kicked off race week by doing an exclusive meet-and-greet at T-Mobile’s Las Vegas Signature Store, where fans got to experience an F1 simulator and other racing-inspired activations while getting up close and personal to one of the sports biggest stars.

Sources indicate that “The fans are the reason our sport is what it is, and you don’t just say it because you have to,” he indicates. “What I love to do is the driving [but] the bonus I get out of it is I have people traveling around the world, supporting me, cheering me on, wanting me to do well. I feel like I need to go out and perform well for them to make it feel like their trip was worth it.”.

Sources indicate that T-Mobile has been part of the F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix since its inaugural race in 2023, and the mobile carrier once again brought its members-only Club Magenta viewing experience to the track this year, while also sponsoring performances from artists like Ja Rule, Gorgon City and Natasha Bedingfield on the T-Mobile Stage. Saturday culminated with the first-ever official post-race show with the Backstreet Boys at Sphere.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

Industry observers note that 2027 is going to be a relatively substantial iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a fresh round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the latest Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will upgrade the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 presently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

It has been revealed that this phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Industry observers note that out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too key – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

In a recent development, it should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

It has been revealed that for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

It has been revealed that I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

In a recent development, lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

Skechers Basketball and Anunoby have just dropped the SKX Nexus “NYC Blue,” a limited-edition pair of sneakers released in the same colorway worn by OG during his now-legendary game-winning tip-in that helped propel New York to an NBA Championship.

The “NYC Blue” colorway pays tribute to the shade of blue seen in the Knicks’ uniforms, while orange laces and accents complete the official team colors.

The shoes themselves feature a breathable and flexible mesh upper, enhanced ankle support, 5GEN midsole cushioning with torsion plate, and a grippy Goodyear outsole for traction on the court. OG’s logo is seen on the sockliner and embroidered on the tongue, with his signature on the heel for an extra personalized touch.

Skechers notes these are shoes designed to boost performance, with lightweight materials, a supportive silhouette, an cushy insole for added comfort, and a “strategically-designed forefoot traction pattern” for precise quick cuts.

Sources indicate that the limited-edition sneakers ship in a custom-designed box and come with a set of collectible enamel pins with Knicks motifs. Skechers has the unisex basketball shoes available in men’s sizes 4 to 17.

While Anunoby’s Player Edition basketball shoe is now available to shop online at Skechers.com, it’s been a long time coming — the SKX Nexus NYC Blue was first revealed for pre-orders in June.

In press materials, Skechers states “This release marks a historic milestone, representing the brand’s first-ever championship win and a defining moment in Skechers Basketball’s rapid rise in the performance space.”.

What is Children of Blood and Bone about?

In a recent development, the first novel in the Legacy of Orïsha trilogy chronicles Zelie’s journey to restore the intrinsic magic to the land after King Saran made a move to purge it, seeing it as a threat and unnatural. Drawning on African mythology, the fantasy setting contains groups of humans that practice magic known as Maji. The Maji divine certain elements, and thus are known by the specific powers they wield, from water workers beckoning tides to those like Zelie’s mother Jumoke, who can summon souls.

Zelie and her brother team up with the son and daughter of King Saran. Prince Inan (Idris) has doubts about taking on his father’s crown and following King Saran’s example directly.

'Wifi Motion Sensing' Can Track Everything You Do Through Your Router

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home.
  • While the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home users might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks.
  • According to recent reports, wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home. "Wifi motion sensing" turns your ISP’s router into a motion detector, letting providers know exactly how many people are in the house, where they are situated, individual movement patterns, and, in some cases, even body shapes that could approximate a person’s identity.

While the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home users might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks. So here’s how wifi routers sense motion, what they can do with it, who has access to the data, and how you can disable it.

According to recent reports, wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances. Those same radio signals are also absorbed and reflected by the human body as they travel in all directions from the router. With the right software, ISPs can track how those wifi signals travel around your room, which can be studied to detect presence and sense motion patterns.

It has been revealed that as long as your ISP’s router model supports this feature natively, it doesn’t require any additional hardware to be installed in your home. For example, Xfinity’s version of the feature pairs your router with five other connected appliances in your room to create oval-shaped sensing zones that can track your presence and movement within those spaces.

Recent findings suggest that it isn’t a latest feature, either—companies like Cognitive Systems and Origin Wireless that supply networking hardware to ISPs have been offering wifi motion sensing for years now, while early research prototypes from the MIT date back at least as far as 2015. In 2025, IEEE updated its Wi-Fi 802.11 standard to include motion sensing and lay out the architectural guidelines for it, which makes it likely that even more routers will now ship with the feature.

Recent findings suggest that in its current consumer form, wifi motion sensing can help you control smart home apparatus like lights or thermostats, get pet safety notifications on your phone, set up a fall alert system for elderly users, and trigger appliances remotely based on human presence. But enabling it carries risks.

Most providers, including Cognitive Systems, claim that the technology isn’t sensitive to identity and can’t be used to track specific individuals. But even if true, that’s more likely to be a product decision rather than a technical limitation. Karlsruhe Institute researchers have shown that even ordinary wifi signals can identify individuals with a 99.5% accuracy.

Also worth noting: ISPs’ legal wording suggests that they may disclose the collected and stored motion data at any time to law enforcement, government agencies, regulators, and courts in response to subpoenas or during an emergency. ISPs may also retain your motion data in the cloud long-term in case they are required to facilitate a subpoena in the future.

Industry observers note that as far as major ISPs are concerned, Xfinity (Comcast) is the only broadband provider that right now offers this feature across its commercial routers on the XB7, XB8, XB9, XB10, MXB1, and XER10 gateways. It’s opted out by default, but in case you or a family member already switched it on, you can disable it again by navigating to Home > WiFi Motion on the Xfinity app, click on the gear icon on the live view page, and tap Remove WiFi Motion.

It has been revealed that verizon Fios customers also had access to a Home Awareness feature on their routers that could be toggled on or off using the MyFios app, but that’s since been discontinued. In an official disclosure published shortly after the discontinuation, Verizon notified customers that it has deleted all associated movement logs from this service and no longer retains any motion data from owners.

Industry observers note that but there are other regional ISPs that offer it, too. For example, Breezeline (Atlantic Broadband) offers a feature called Motion within its Plume-powered application that alerts customers when movement is detected in their homes, among its other features. MidCo, a telecom organization in the Upper Midwest, has a feature called Sense which can be toggled on or off using the MidCo Wi-Fi app. Plume, ADT-owned Origin Wireless, and Airties—all of whom supply technology to ISPs—have also been marketing motion sensing to customers for the last few years.

If you’re unsure if your wifi router or ISP has motion sensing features or opts you in by default, look for a feature called “Sense,” “Motion,” or equivalent in your broadband’s mobile app. Exact steps differ greatly from one ISP to another, so it’s best not to assume that they will all opt you out by default, or that they collect the same types of data. With the 802.11bf revision to IEEE standards in 2025, this technology will be accessible to even more router manufacturers, so expect adoption to grow among internet providers as well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the last day of principal photography on Avengers: Doomsday, revered actor Patrick Stewart, who reprised his role of Professor Charles Xavier for the film, stood up and gave a moving speech to the cast and crew. It would be his last day on a film set anywhere, according to his colleagues.

“We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was,” Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige said in an interview with Entertainment Weekly.

Recent findings suggest that anthony and Joe Russo, who helmed the last two Avengers films, 2018’s Infinity War and 2019’s Endgame, also felt the impact of the celebrated actor’s words that day. “I think it was in the back of all of our heads, we may never see him on set again,” Anthony told the outlet, calling the atmosphere that day as “very emotional.”.

When addressing those he had worked side-by-side with, Stewart highlighted his character Xavier, whose empathy for others offered a source of comfort and security. “It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence — for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew,” Anthony remarked. “It was someone who was really being challenged in a very deep way on a health level, showing up and doing that. For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.”.

Feige confirmed to EW that he and the Russos are working on planning a tribute to Stewart. “We’re long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us,” he noted. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.”.

Stewart died at age 86 on Oct. 28 in his Los Angeles home. His prolific career spanned decades with work across more than five dozen films and over 50 television appearances, from X-Men and Star Trek to Dune and American Dad. Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday, which is set to hit theaters on Dec. 18, will see Stewart and Ian McKellen reprise their roles from past X-Men films as Professor X and Magneto, respectively. Doom is set to be portrayed by Robert Downey Jr., returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe after previously playing Tony Stark/Iron Man, alongside a large ensemble cast of actors from the past several years of Marvel films and TV shows.

10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone.
  • This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually.
  • There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags customers should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”.

You can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to enhancement it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

Some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

In a recent development, to make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

According to recent reports, if you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

It has been revealed that to set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

You can quickly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

It has been revealed that you might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Industry observers note that find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

Sources indicate that if you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Sources indicate that map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

According to recent reports, if you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

Go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal grand jury has indicted Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan Markle, on charges that he knowingly possessed child sexual abuse material — including images where Markle himself was photographed with prepubescent children.

Markle remains in custody in Florida and has been charged with two counts of possession of child pornography. He is expected to be arraigned in United States District Court in Los Angeles in the coming weeks. According to prosecutors, Markle knowingly possessed 35 mm negatives that included at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor who had not yet attained the age of 12 years old.

The allegations against Markle Sr. first emerged in October when his son Thomas Markle Jr. reported to authorities that he found the inappropriate images at his father’s home in the Philippines. Markle Jr. reportedly told detectives he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images where Markle Sr. was living.

Recent findings suggest that in early November, Markle was arrested in Florida amid the investigation and charged with one count of possession of child pornography. Weeks later, the Philippine National Police filed three charges with prosecutors in the city of Cebu, where Markle reportedly lived until May, according to ITV News. The charges included two counts of offering, distributing, selling, exporting, or importing child sex abuse material, and one count of possessing child sex abuse material. While the investigation into Markle originated with his son’s claims in the Philippines, U.S. investigators picked it up after learning that Markle rented two storage units in Los Angeles. According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, from those units FBI special agents seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sex abuse material. Several images allegedly highlighted Markle with children who were either naked or in various states of undress.

If convicted, Markle faces a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison on each count.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Recent findings suggest that right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

Sources indicate that the X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#97023. Latest Update: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?
