Gödel Enigma

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Helsinki

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gödel's solitary work was the single most crucial factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine.
  • Sources indicate that the development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work.
  • Deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gödel's solitary work was the single most crucial factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine. His work led to precise notions of algorithmic computability from which a direct path leads to the first theoretical ideas of a computer in the work of Alan Turing in 1936 and John von Neumann some years later.

Sources indicate that the development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work. He published in 1967 a collection of original papers under the title From Frege to Gödel: The Development of Mathematical Logic 1879-1931. There was, however, no attempt at organised historical work with the sources. Such detailed work is still in a very early state and crucial sources for the development of logic remain unexplored.

Deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered. Comparison to a parallel and partly overlapping development is illuminating. Quantum mechanics, as well as foundations of mathematics, received a decisive impetus around the year 1900, with Planck's discovery of the quantum of action, and the discovery of Russell's paradox and Hilbert's idea of formalisation. All of these developments led to a well-established theoretical account by the early 1930s, right before the Nazi takeover in Germany: quantum mechanics in the second part of the 1920s in the work of the Göttingers Heisenberg and Born, logic and foundations with the full development of first-order logic by the early 1930s by the Göttingers Hilbert, Bernays, and Gentzen, assisted mainly by Gödel's striking discoveries.

Historical work on the development of quantum mechanics began in the 1960s in a massive effort in which every conceivable source was unearthed and made available in several hundred microfilm reels, the Archive for the History of Quantum Physics.

Sadly, nothing of this kind was ever done with logic and foundations. Our present information society owes a part of its existence to a well-hidden but essential line of development. There are several thousand pages of notes by Gödel waiting to be studied, written in Similarly, extensive notes for lecture courses during the crucial years, written by Paul Bernays, the central driving force in foundational study around 1930, as well as over five thousand contemporaneous letters exist in the Bernays archive. These have been exploited only sporadically. The fate of many other sources, such as the papers of Gerhard Gentzen and Rose Rand, has been similar.

The main aims of our project are twofold:.

Understanding Gödel's unpublished papers requires a combination of mastery of the logical details and the application of professional standards of historical-foundational research to the source material, which, in addition, is only accessible to a reader trained in stenographic writing. So far, much of this work remains to be done. There are two exceptions: the transcription of Gödel's so-called "Zilsel lecture" in Vienna in January 1938 and his Göttingen lecture on the consistency of the continuum hypothesis of December 1939, both published in the third volume of Gödel's Collected Works. Both of these texts were lecture notes, relatively finished in comparison to the private notes. More recently, much effort has been dedicated to producing transcriptions of Gödel's philosophical notebooks that he called "Max Phil," or Philosophical Maxims, in order to better understand Gödel the philosopher. Our project will provide ample material for future generations of philosophers and logicians to complement the picture given by the Philosophical Maxims as well as other works of Gödel's published so far.

In a recent development, the project consists of theoretically oriented basic research. It uses special methods for the study of mostly unpublished primary sources, the contemporary methods of logic and foundational study to aid in their interpretation, up-to-date formal methods for the development of research themes suggested by the sources, and scholarly methodological standards of historical-foundational research.

The main sources comprise a number of series of notebooks, all written in shorthand and logical symbolism, left virtually untouched except for the Max Phil series:.

Gödel's notebooks have some overlap in themes, ideas and results that are presented in Max Phil or Resultate Grundlagen often appearing in less finished form in the Arbeitshefte, to give an example. Gödel was meticulous about keeping his notebooks, and they contain detailed lists of contents from which we can infer that he did reread them. There is a separate list of "Progress" entries, in which he summed both his achievements and objectives in numbered points in the Arbeitshefte.

Tech Report: Tidal Is the First Streaming Platform to Ban AI Music

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (428 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service.
  • According to recent reports, on Tuesday, Tidal revealed plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely.
  • This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You have a few options when it comes to choosing a music streaming service. If you own an iPhone and a Mac, you might be tempted by Apple Music; if you have more friends on Spotify, you may feel that's the best platform for you. But if your goal is avoiding AI music as much as humanly possible, there appears to be a fresh uncontested winner: Tidal.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, Tidal revealed plans to ban AI music from its platform entirely. Starting Dec. 9, the tech giant will begin taking steps to remove music it believes is entirely made with AI. Tidal notes it thinks the move “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”.

This isn't the first stand Tidal has taken against AI-generated music. Back in July, the firm declared that it would start labeling songs completely made with AI, as well as remove tracks it found to be "fraudulent and deceptive." Other platforms have similar policies, or are rolling out similar features. Apple Music, for example, is working on AI labels for its app, too, and Spotify has pushed back on AI to some degree. However, this most recent move makes Tidal the first music streaming service to outright ban AI-generated music from its catalog.

Robert Anderson, Tidal's Music Lead, posted on X about the change. According to Anderson, Tidal identified 43% of the tracks it received in the last 90 days were AI-generated. Per the company's blueprint, Tidal will remove 29 million songs by the beginning of 2027, roughly 80,000 to 85,000 removals per day. Some 96% of Tidal's AI-generated songs have zero plays whatsoever.

Recent findings suggest that I wouldn't be surprised to see other music streaming services follow suit, particularly Apple Music. Despite rolling out AI-powered features over the past couple of years, including Apple Music's AI-generated playlists, Apple has taken some stands against AI-generated material in general. The latest Apple TV intro was shot in-camera with practical effects, in an era where the organization could have easily generated something with AI. If other companies proposal to follow Tidal's lead here, my money's on Apple being first in line.

However, as it stands, Tidal is the only streaming service that supports this initiative. Soon enough, it'll be the sole music app you can use with near-zero ambiguity that the music you're listening to was at least mostly created by humans. (What a sentence.) Avoiding AI-generated music can be tricky, frustrating, and, frankly, exhausting. If that's key to you, Tidal might just be your upcoming pick.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic notes.

  • Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end.
  • Recent findings suggest that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii.
  • A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Recent findings suggest that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the latest social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

Sources indicate that the premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the indicates share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

It has been revealed that the 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

Sources indicate that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Industry observers note that A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the substantial city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their latest home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent findings suggest that this latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated highlights in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

According to recent reports, kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense newly introduced forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've been thinking about picking up a Bluetooth tracker to keep tabs on your keys, luggage, or other valuables, now is probably the best time to get one. Apple introduced its second-generation AirTag 2 earlier this year, but the tracker is already down to its lowest price yet for Black Friday. You can now grab a single Apple AirTag for just $18 at Amazon, down from its usual $29 price.

Recent findings suggest that and if you're an Android user, there's a pretty good deal for you as well. The Moto Tag 2, which offers many of the same features as Apple's AirTag, is currently down to just $19 at Amazon.

It has been revealed that apple's latest AirTag features an improved Precision Finding range, a 50% louder speaker, and up to a year of battery life. It works seamlessly with Apple's Find My network and is now down to just $18 (38% off).

It has been revealed that the second-generation AirTag offers up to 1.5 times the Precision Finding range of its predecessor. Apple has also upgraded the built-in speaker, making it 50% louder than the original AirTag, and features a fresh, more distinctive chime. this makes it a lot easier to locate your belongings when they're nearby.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest reasons to get an AirTag over most other Apple Find My-compatible trackers, though, is Precision Finding. While other key finders and trackers also let you locate your belongings through the Find My app warn you if you leave something behind, the AirTag takes things a step further with its ultra-wideband (UWB) technology.

If you've misplaced your keys somewhere around the house, for example, you can simply open the Find My app on a compatible iPhone, and it'll show you exactly which direction to walk in and how far away your AirTag is — rather than just relying on a sound to locate it.

It has been revealed that and if you're planning to put AirTags on multiple belongings, there's also a deal on the AirTag four-pack, which is currently down to $79 from its usual $99 price. That said, at $18 apiece, buying four individual AirTags actually works out slightly cheaper.

According to recent reports, if you're on the Android side of things, the Moto Tag 2 is arguably one of the best alternatives to Apple's AirTag. Much like Apple's AirTag, the Moto Tag 2 features ultra-wideband technology, which means you can use precision finding on compatible Android phones to pinpoint the location of your items.

It also works with Google's Find Hub network, so you can locate your items even when they're outside your phone's Bluetooth range.

In a recent development, the Moto Tag 2 brings an AirTag-like tracking experience to Android with UWB Precision Finding, Google's Find Hub integration, over 600 days of battery life, and IP68 water resistance. It's at the moment down to just $19 from $30.

But there are a couple of things the Moto Tag 2 does even better than Apple's AirTag. For starters, Motorola claims over 600 days of battery life, which is considerably longer than the year of battery life Apple promises. You can also use the button on the Moto Tag 2 as a remote camera shutter, which is particularly handy for taking group photos or selfies.

You also get features like left-behind notifications and an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, so you don't have to worry too much about attaching it to your backpack or other belongings you carry outdoors.

On the whole, I think $20 is a pretty reasonable amount to spend on something that could save you a lot of trouble if you ever lose your keys or luggage. And if you've been holding off on buying an item tracker for your phone, now's a pretty good time to get one, regardless of whether you use an iPhone or an Android phone.

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the upcoming Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

The Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that debuted a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

It has been revealed that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

#96940. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3547 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Sources indicate that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell states. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen reveals my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics manufacturer. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

According to recent reports, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

Sources indicate that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Sources indicate that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

According to recent reports, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sources indicate that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team indicated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

It has been revealed that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga notes, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

According to recent reports, about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga states. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Industry observers note that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Latest York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

It has been revealed that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Industry observers note that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics manufacturer XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

According to recent reports, “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Sources indicate that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more vital than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Industry observers note that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” states neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Recent findings suggest that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Recent findings suggest that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu notes.

According to recent reports, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” indicates neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

In a recent development, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra states. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

It has been revealed that if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

Recent findings suggest that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

In a recent development, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

It has been revealed that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

In a recent development, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he indicates. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Sources indicate that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga indicates they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person firm into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cupertino is one of those TV highlights that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

In a recent development, the film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that the true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that if your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Everyday displays, such as the ones found in your phone, laptop, or television, require a constant power draw to maintain an image.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers from the ARC Centre of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS) are the first to report a reflective display based on Antimony Selenide that can hold an image for months without being powered.

Everyday displays, such as the ones found in your phone, laptop, or television, require a constant power draw to maintain an image. However, now, reflective displays are emerging as a sustainable alternative that could offer near zero power consumption while maintaining an image.

In a cross-node collaboration at TMOS, researchers from the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) and the Australian National University (ANU) have demonstrated the promise of Antimony Selenide (Sb2Se3) a material for lower-power displays by building and testing a reflective platform capable of retaining an image for months without power, being reliably reusable, and offering a wide colour gamut.

The lead researcher, Dr Phuong Yen Le, says, âThis is a newly introduced way to create energy-efficient displays.â.

Their study was published in Advanced Photonics Research.

The key to the latest display technology is an unusual type of material that Dr Le has been excited to study for a long time: phase change materials (PCMs).

Unlike most materials, PCMs can be rearranged repeatedly at the atomic level by selectively applying stimuli, such as heat, light, or electricity.

These stimuli can be used to rearrange the structure of the atoms, or âphaseâ, of the material from amorphous (irregular arrangements of atoms) to crystalline (highly ordered arrangements of atoms) and back again.

It is this capacity to be reordered that has interested Dr Le for a long time.

Recent findings suggest that âI think phase change materials are really, really cool [â¦] Most materials always stay in one structure, so if you choose crystallised arrangement during fabrication [â¦] any application is going to be fixed to that material structure. But these [PCMs] can change so you get different optical and electrical properties.â.

It has been revealed that what makes Antimony Selenide desirable among PCMs is its non-volatility. Once it changes phase, it is locked and does not require continuous power to maintain its state.

This is a promising tool, but to make a display, Dr Le and the research teams first needed to understand how best to produce a range of colours and shades with PCMs.

One of the reasons for choosing Antimony Selenide how significantly its interaction with light changed between the crystalline and amorphous forms.

In a recent development, light travelling through the different phases moves at different speeds and is absorbed to different degrees. It was these effects that could be leveraged to produce different colours.

From Dr Leâs perspective, understanding the relationship between phase and colour was the main thrust of the research.

In a recent development, âThis work is really about characterising Antimony Selenide. We wanted to understand how changes in its structure affect its optical properties and how those optical changes can be used to create different colours in a device.â.

Combining the investigation of phase with different thicknesses of the Antimony Selenide, the researchers produced colours ranging from deep blues through to greys and oranges.

But Dr Le says this is just the start of the colour possibilities.

âAt the moment, this structure only gives us a limited range of colours. The next step is to understand what changes to the deviceâs structure will make more colours accessible and expand the colour gamut.â.

So, how is this material rearranged at the atomic level to produce these colours? It is a little like trying to change glass into quartz and back again repeatedly.

Erasing the display was done by heating the material to ~200Â°C uniformly; at this temperature, the atoms have enough energy to move around and find upcoming positions and orientations.

At these high temperatures, atoms can migrate into the most stable positions, which tend to be crystals due to the dense packing of their regular structure.

This process is known as annealing, and it resets the display with a uniform blank image.

Then, to draw images on the blank screen, co-author Dr Shvedov used short laser pulses, like drawing with a laser instead of a pencil.

The laser pulses add just enough energy to get the atoms moving again and into irregular arrangements, but crucially, this is done quickly.

As the regions hit with the laser cool down quickly, the atoms freeze in their latest irregular arrangement before without a chance to settle back into their crystalline configuration.

This leaves them fixed in their amorphous phase, resulting in different coloured regions.

Putting it all to the test, a variety of images, including a map of Australia, the TMOS logo, and a koala, were drawn and erased on the display.

The researchers found that there was no residual image after annealing, even when inspected under a 5Ã magnification microscope.

But even more surprisingly, the image of a koala was imprinted on the material and left for three months under ambient conditions without any noticeable change.

And in fact, Dr Le tells us it has lasted even longer.

Industry observers note that âActually, I still have that image with me. It still looks the same a year later.â.

These were promising results for developing this display technology further, and Dr Le already had some avenues to cover to get to true commercial energy-efficient displays.

In a recent development, âRight now, it uses a laser. It needs to be a fully electrical device as well. So presently Iâm working on testing the electrical characteristics of the material [â¦] and if we want to have more colour, we may need to change the structure.â.

Nonvolatile, Rewritable, Multilevel Reflective Displays Based on Antimony Selenide Thin Films.

In a recent development, phuong Y. Le, Vladlen Shvedov, Yana Izdebskaya, Peter F. M. Elango, Krishna Murali, Ilya V. Shadrivov, Sharath Sriram, Madhu Bhaskaran.

Advanced Photonics Research, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1002/adpr.70305.

Reflective display technologies are emerging as a sustainable alternative to traditional emissive systems, offering the potential for near-zero static power consumption. Chalcogenide phase change materials, with their nonvolatile nature and reversible structural transformations between their phases, represent promising candidates for such applications. Here, we demonstrate a multilevel, rewritable display platform based on a thin film of the phase-change material antimony selenide (Sb2Se3). By integrating Sb2Se3 into a multilayer interference stack, the resonant optical response can be precisely modulated through thickness engineering and active control of the materialâs crystallinity. We demonstrate that nanosecond laser pulses can induce multiple intermediate states, expanding the accessible color gamut beyond binary switching. The devices exhibit excellent rewritability and long-term stability, with images persisting for months without degradation. These findings position Sb2Se3 as a promising candidate for next-generation, nonvolatile displays and high-density optical information storage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

According to recent reports, this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful.
  • In a recent development, and focus on presentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

In a recent development, and focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:.

In a recent development, when time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Recent findings suggest that include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”.

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

It has been revealed that sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:.

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

Recent findings suggest that spiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

According to recent reports, cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

It has been revealed that sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Sources indicate that wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Industry observers note that hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.
