  • We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created.
  • The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, greyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.

Example POST to loginSrp1 and response.

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested.

Industry observers note that 2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant.

They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

It has been revealed that 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.

The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

In a recent development, once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.

Sources indicate that between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a upcoming certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

Sources indicate that the bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.

Excerpt from exploit.py -  This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.

2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.

Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.

2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and introduced pull_.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.

Sources indicate that excerpt from pull_.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.

2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.

2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.

In a recent development, 2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.

2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.

In a recent development, note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.

All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.

Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt.

One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.

After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.

2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.

Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.

Wired headphones proved to be a real surprise category this year, and Sony recently cashed in by releasing the MDR-3R wired headphones, which proved so popular that they've sold out three times since launching mere weeks ago.

Good news for you, fans of the 80s: The Sony MDR-3R are back in stock, so you better act fast before they sell out again.

A post shared by Tom's Guide (@tomsguide).

The Sony MDR-3R headphones are right now only available in silver with orange and blue earpads (you get a set of each). The "Stranger Things" limited edition models are still sold out.

As iconic as the Sony Walkman, Sony's headphones were that era's AirPods; instantly recognizable by anyone who spotted them on the street. The 2026 version of these trades in the 3.5mm headphone jack for a USB-C port, which makes more sense given how many smartphones have ditched dedicated audio ports. It also has a set of inline volume controls as well as a microphone, so you can use them to take phone calls.

Now, don't expect stellar audio quality out of these, but our own Kate Kozuch took a pair for a spin, and said that they're definitely more for the look than the fidelity. This is a nostalgia play more than anything else.

Sources indicate that as of this writing, Sony is estimating a ship date of December 5, so you'll have to wait a week or two before you get them. But, if you're planning on gifting them, it'll leave you plenty of time to get them wrapped.

  • It has been revealed that the underlying series goes back to Euler, but has been rearranged to exploit more efficient evaluation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this post introduces a upcoming algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of \(\pi\) without computing the preceding digits. It beats the standard term-by-term evaluations of Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP), Bellard, and Huvent on operation count. Even against Huvent’s eight-term formula, the savings are about 61% fewer divisions and 38% fewer full modular exponentiations.

The key insights come from the following identity:.

It has been revealed that the underlying series goes back to Euler, but has been rearranged to exploit more efficient evaluation. Collecting its terms by odd denominator lets us share the arithmetic in two places:.

Industry observers note that the common denominator \(M=2k+1\) means we can add four remainders and divide once. The surprise is that we don’t have to compute those remainders independently either. The gaps between the exponents are small multiples of \(k\) plus constants, so one starting power and the step \(2^k\bmod M\) let us reach the others by multiplication.

In a recent development, two full exponentiations modulo \(3M\) serve both denominators \(M\) and \(3M\). That gives us up to eight powers of two, and we still only divide once.

Industry observers note that together, these two tricks save about a million full exponentiations per million hexadecimal places skipped compared with Huvent, before any machine-specific optimization. In practice, this algorithm leads to an implementation that runs in nearly 40% less wall-clock time.

Industry observers note that to see where the savings come from, let’s recall the BBP trick. To skip \(n\) hex digits, shift \(\pi\) left by \(d=4n\) bits and take the fractional part. Shifting by \(d\) bits adds \(d\) to each exponent, so we’re left adding and subtracting terms of the form \(2^E/N\). When \(E\ge 0\), write \(2^E=qN+r\). Then \(2^E/N=q+r/N\), and we don’t care about \(q\): it’s an integer. Even at \(d=4{,}000{,}000\), we can compute \(r=2^E\bmod N\) without ever constructing a four-million-bit numerator.

Industry observers note that the terms with \(E<0\) make up the tail. They decay geometrically, so we sum them directly, keeping enough guard bits to settle the last digit we want.

The above is essentially the BBP trick, and is the basis for three decades of digit extraction algorithms.

As such, when I was programmatically looking for efficient BBP-formula, I ranked them by how many fractions I’d have to evaluate to reach a given digit. Each fraction in the main loop costs me a modular exponentiation and a division. Bellard’s formula advances 10 bits for every seven fractions; Huvent’s formula advances 12 bits for every eight. After finding Huvent’s formula independently, I’ve tried feverishly to find one with a better ratio, without success. So I looked toward ways of optimizing existing series.

Recent findings suggest that one clue tipped me off. There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s terse derivation. He has one sum in powers of \(1/4\) and another in powers of \(1/1024\). Since \(4^5=1024\), splitting the first sum into five progressions lets him write both sums in powers of \(1/1024\). What if, instead of lining up the powers, we lined up the denominators?

It has been revealed that lining up denominators seemed hard with the many-term series of Bellard and Huvent. One good place I found to try this is a series Euler wrote down in 1779, as noted by Craig-Wood, who used it himself to write an extraction program1. In Euler’s original formulation, there are six rows:.

Takahashi writes this more straightforwardly as two sums distinguished by their exponential factors:.

Industry observers note that notice the denominators of the fractions. Since \(4m+2=2(2m+1)\), we can halve the numerator of the middle fraction and leave \(2m+1\) in the denominator. As \(m\) runs over the nonnegative integers, \(2m+1\) gives every positive odd integer. The other two progressions, \(4m+1\) and \(4m+3\), split that same list between them. So each odd denominator appears twice in each sum.

In a recent development, for example, consider the denominator 13. The first progression hits it at \(m=3\); the middle one hits it at \(m=6\), where the original denominator was 26. That’s two contributions from the sum in powers of \(1/64\) and two from the sum in powers of \(1/1024\). The powers are different, but all four numerators can be added before we divide by 13. We can collect terms this way for every odd denominator.

Recent findings suggest that to derive the boxed formula directly, we can start with a multiplication of Gaussian integers: \((3-i)^2(7-i)=50(1-i)\). Taking complex arguments gives Hutton’s arctangent identity from the 18th century:.

Recent findings suggest that bellard lists this identity as equation (7). His logarithm trick works on both angles: \(1-(1+i)/4=(3-i)/4\), and \(1-(1+i)/8=(7-i)/8\). So if we put.

Sources indicate that then \(I_2=\arctan(1/3)\), \(I_3=\arctan(1/7)\), and we want \(\pi=8I_2+4I_3\). Every time \(j\) goes up by four, \((1+i)^j/2^{uj}\) is multiplied by \(-4/2^{4u}\). That’s \(-1/64\) in the first sum and \(-1/1024\) in the second.

Industry observers note that for an odd denominator \(N=2k+1\), the two contributions in each logarithm come from \(j=N\) and \(j=2N\). All further doublings give multiples of four, where \((1+i)^j\) is real and contributes nothing. At \(j=N\) the imaginary part of \((1+i)^N\) is \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^k\); at \(j=2N\) we’re looking at \((2i)^N=(-1)^k 2^N i\). At \(j=N\), the first logarithm multiplies the imaginary part by \(8/2^{2(2k+1)}\), giving the numerator term \((-1)^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}2^{1-3k}\). Collect the other three contributions in the same way and we have the boxed formula.

After the shift by \(d\), that is, multiplying the sum by \(2^d\), the four exponents, in the order we wrote them, are.

Call a power active if its exponent is nonnegative. The slowest-decaying exponent is \(E_1\), which stays nonnegative up to \(k=\lfloor(d+1)/3\rfloor\). That’s about \(d/3\) odd denominators, and we divide just once for each one. Even the largest modulus is only \(2d/3+O(1)\), compared with about \(d\) for Bellard or Huvent, and \(2d\) for the original BBP formula.

It has been revealed that as for the remainders \(r_j=2^{E_j}\bmod N\), notice that the middle two exponents differ by \(k\). If we already have \(r_3\) and \(x=2^k\bmod N\), then \(r_2\) is just \(xr_3\bmod N\). In fact, we can step from the smallest exponent up to the largest:.

Industry observers note that start at the smallest active power. We pay for one full exponentiation to get it and one to get \(x\); the rest are a handful of multiplications. Past \(k\approx d/5\) only \(E_1\) is active, so don’t bother computing \(x\).2 That’s two exponentiations for the first \(d/5\) denominators and one for the remaining \(d/3-d/5\), or about \(8d/15\) altogether.

According to recent reports, so far we’ve paid for one division by 13 and another by 39. Call the signed sums of their active powers \(A\) and \(B\). Since 39 is three times 13, their combined contribution is.

We only want the fractional part, so we can compute both numerators modulo 39, take the remainder of \(3A+B\), and divide by 39 just once.

Now consider the step powers. For 13 the index is 6; for 39 it’s 19. Since \(19=3\cdot6+1\), once we have \(x=2^6\bmod39\), we get the step for 39 by cubing and doubling: \(2^{19}\equiv2x^3\pmod{39}\).

Industry observers note that in general, tripling a denominator \(M=2k+1\) changes its index from \(k\) to \(3k+1\). Substitute that index into the four exponents above to get the partner’s exponents. Now read the active exponents from both numerators in increasing order. The common \(d\) cancels in every gap, leaving a small multiple of \(k\) plus a constant. We need just two full exponentiations modulo \(3M\): one for the first power in the list and one for the step \(2^k\). Multiplication takes us up the rest of the list.

According to recent reports, we never need to compute the step just for \(3M\). Its largest exponent, \(d-2-9k\), is smaller than the second exponent for \(M\), \(d-1-5k\). If \(3M\) has even one active power, \(M\) already has at least two.

Sources indicate that we don’t want to pair 39 with 13 and then pair it again with 117. So we start pairs only at odd \(M\) not divisible by three. If \(3M\) has an active power, we take it with \(M\); otherwise we process \(M\) alone. Odd multiples of nine, like 117, stay unpaired.

The denominators that no longer need their own turn are precisely the odd multiples of three that aren’t multiples of nine. That’s two out of every nine odd denominators, both where we need one exponentiation and where we need two. Multiplying the counts above by \(7/9\) gives about \(7d/27\) divisions and \(56d/135\) full exponentiations, compared to \(2d/3\) of each for Huvent.

Here is how the formulas compare in terms of how far into \(\pi\) we get per expensive arithmetic operation, expressed as “bits per operation”:.

Recent findings suggest that I implemented both the algorithm of this post and Huvent using AVX-512 IFMA. Here’s how long each took to extract 12 hex digits on my computer.

Returning to the pair 13 and 39, while 39 is active, I never reduce modulo 13: changing the numerator for 13 by a multiple of 13 changes its tripled contribution by a multiple of 39. So I do all the squaring and multiplying modulo 39. Since 39 is odd, I can compute its inverse modulo a power of two once and reuse it for every Montgomery multiplication in the pair. I triple the numerator for 13, add the one for 39, and convert back from Montgomery form just once for the final division.

There’s a nice trick inside each exponentiation, too. Suppose a Montgomery reduction leaves \(-14\) modulo 39. Normally I’d add 39 to get 25. But if I’m going to square it next, 14 is just as good: \(14^2\equiv25^2\pmod{39}\). Even if the current exponent bit calls for doubling first, the next square still erases the sign. So for all but the last bit, I use vector absolute values instead of correcting the sign. On the last bit I do the usual reduction, since the numerator needs the actual residue rather than its negative. That change made the exponentiation loop about 8% faster on Zen 5.

Recent findings suggest that each vector lane handles a different odd modulus. I batch moduli with the same set of active powers so that one lane doesn’t sit idle while another steps through three extra residues. The hardware multiplies 52-bit inputs, so the largest modulus matters: ours is about \(2d/3\), compared with \(d\) for Huvent. That lets us reach about 50% farther into \(\pi\) before we need wider arithmetic.

Sources indicate that I originally went looking for a series with fewer fractions per bit. If you evaluate every fraction separately, Euler’s series actually needs more fractions per bit than Huvent’s, so it has been easy to pass over. Sharing the modular arithmetic across common and paired denominators is what makes it faster, and I suspect similar tricks apply to other BBP-type series.

His implementation evaluates 21 fractions separately for every 30 bits of offset. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that there’s a way to thin out the far end of the loop even more. At \(j=4m+3\), the real and imaginary parts of \((1+i)^j\) are opposites. Add the real part of each logarithm and the two slow powers cancel for \(N\equiv3\pmod4\). We still have to subtract the real logarithms we added, using series for \(\log(1+2^{-2})\), \(\log(1+2^{-3})\), and \(\log(1-2^{-4})\). That leaves half as many moduli above \(d/2\), at the cost of more streams of powers to juggle below it. ↩︎.

#96919. Tech Report: Macrohistory in Six Facts

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)

Tech Report: Macrohistory in Six Facts

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Basilhalperin

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models.
  • Recent findings suggest that can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts?
  • What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most key theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).”.

Recent findings suggest that can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts.

What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’.

In richer countries, on average people are happier.

Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer:.

Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die:.

Industry observers note that are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less:.

According to recent reports, more intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more:.

Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person:.

And all of this is correlation not causation.

But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing.

This is the most important fact about human history.

We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth.

Everyone used to be poor. This is the most crucial fact about macro history.

It has been revealed that why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape:.

This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250.

Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence.

Industry observers note that we lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until:.

The Industrial Revolution was the single most vital event in human history.

We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate.

According to recent reports, the Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in macro history. It also brought about:.

According to recent reports, the growth explosion from the Industrial Revolution did not take place everywhere and all at once. Many countries did not see faster growth and rising GDP per person until much later – and many still have not seen these much at all.

But let’s talk first about the frontier.

In a recent development, this is the most important fact in modern macro. Growth at the technological frontier – measured here as GDP per person in the United States – has been a shockingly steady 2% per year for the last 150 years.

You can see a temporary blip down for the Great Depression, but otherwise the trend has been remarkably constant.

Running water, electricity, automobiles, computers, the web – all show up here as a continuation of a steady 2% per year trend.

What about the rest of the world?

In a recent development, the figure here has on the X-axis, income per person per day. You can see, for example, that even the poorest 11% of people in the United States have on average a higher income than the median person in Bangladesh or Ethiopia.

Sources indicate that income varies enormously across countries. Those of us born in the United States are so, so lucky.

Well, are we stuck with these enormous differences? No:.

Here again we see the United States up top as the frontier.

Japan and South Korea, at the turn of the 20th century, were ∼as poor as sub-Saharan Africa is today. But Japan and South Korea caught up close to the United States. There are growth miracles.

Sources indicate that but there are also growth disasters. Argentina at the turn of the 20th century was one of the richest countries in the world. But it has stagnated, relative to the frontier. A classic basket case.

And there are countries like Nigeria, which have never experienced much sustained growth at all.

According to recent reports, what should we expect of the future? This takes us to the most fun fact, the most speculative:.

Over the long sweep of history, aggregate GDP growth is speeding up.

Industry observers note that what I have plotted here is how long it takes for world GDP to double. This goes back to 1 million years ago. Measuring GDP in 1 million BC is hard, but for our purposes I feel good about these numbers.

We’ve gone from doubling every 100,000 years down to a modern doubling time of every 35 or so years.

Now, to the natural question: what should we expect about growth in the future?

I think it really comes down to: which prior do you want to anchor to?

Do you want to anchor to the last 150 years or so, with our constant 2% growth and doubling every 35 years?

Or do you want to anchor to the long sweep of macrohistory, where growth has been speeding up?

Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff?

This is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.

I found these “Six Significant Facts of Macrohistory” particularly useful as framing when teaching my undergrad macro course for the first time last fall: teaching GDP construction (fact 0), the Malthusian model (fact 1), the theories of the Industrial Revolution (fact 2), the Solow model (facts 3-5), and the endogenous growth model (fact 6).

It was pedagogically very useful to have this catechism of the Six Facts to review at the start of many classes, to anchor the students to where we were in the course.

Industry observers note that it was also useful for me, for setting a target for the bare minimum that students might remember in a decade. Do I expect them to remember the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model? No. Or even the idea of income vs. substitution effects? For the vast majority – no, not really.

According to recent reports, can I hope that they pick up a gut-level sense, in their bones, that everyone used to be poor? That’s an extremely important idea, a realistic goal, and yet an idea that the vast majority of people do not know or have not properly internalized.

Recent findings suggest that I also think the Six Major Facts of Macrohistory is a useful attempt to condense “what should any well-informed civilian know about macro and macrohistory”. E.g. my microeconomist wife, or my parents.

In a recent development, what are the runner-up facts not listed here? Structural transformation and urbanization? The demographic transition? Women’s emancipation or rising health would be the natural top candidates, but are captured (if perhaps buried) in Fact 0.

Again, underlying these figures is the astounding work of generations of economic historians, demographers, national statistical agencies, and others.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….
  • Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler states that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler states that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

It has been revealed that I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

Sources indicate that the “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler indicates, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

Sources indicate that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting manufacturer to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

It has been revealed that the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

Industry observers note that TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

Recent findings suggest that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

It has been revealed that chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

Recent findings suggest that “The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Fresh York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

Sources indicate that the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, stated to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd fresh design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

The iPhone 17e was released in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but states that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.
  • Sources indicate that microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos.
  • Industry observers note that jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Sources indicate that microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

Industry observers note that jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

Diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

Sources indicate that charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

Microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft states cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

Silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also looks to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

Henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

Earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach users worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security problems, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

Last week, Nadella remarked that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

Recent findings suggest that iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

Sources indicate that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

It has been revealed that with iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically enhancement across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:.

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

In a recent development, AT&T, meanwhile, has no aims to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier remarked that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

It has been revealed that in my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents ….

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

Recent findings suggest that A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum stated:.

In a recent development, AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce upcoming ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Recent findings suggest that meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve notable actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but indicates other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a upcoming blog post, Meta says:.

Industry observers note that muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it indicates you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

Sources indicate that at the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that data centers already use light in networking.
  • Recent findings suggest that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Recent findings suggest that data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

Recent findings suggest that the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Industry observers note that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” notes Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Fresh Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Recent findings suggest that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How massive do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also crucial to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

Sources indicate that the Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Sources indicate that lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

It has been revealed that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Industry observers note that bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen states, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The firm is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Sources indicate that free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

According to recent reports, “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” states Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

Recent findings suggest that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the firm announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main concern is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch notes, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Recent findings suggest that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” claims Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the manufacturer believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch notes.

It has been revealed that the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the manufacturer’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

Industry observers note that lightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to swiftly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the tech giant’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

According to recent reports, the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Fresh indicates. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

According to recent reports, some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New notes that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

In a recent development, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he notes. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

In a recent development, whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”.

Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.

Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it indicates is the largest ever for Latin America. It will back 20 to 30 AI startups, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, at a time when only 14 venture funds have closed in the region this year.

Kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The firm notes it is the largest early-stage fund ever raised for the region.

Industry observers note that the fund, Kaszek’s seventh for early-stage deals, beat its $600M target. Its last one, closed in 2023, raised $540M. Washington University in St. Louis and the Wellcome Trust are among the backers.

Sources indicate that kaszek prepares to back 20 to 30 companies, starting at pre-seed and seed. It will keep about 60% of the money for their later rounds.

Industry observers note that most of the focus is on what Kaszek calls the “application layer” of AI. That means startups using language models in fields such as finance, health care and online marketplaces. Co-founder Hernán Kazah told Bloomberg he sees the most room in services for businesses.

It has been revealed that “It’s a more natural fit for the types of problems that exist in Latin America,” Kazah said. Many firms there still rely on manual processes, he added, and services can be costly or hard to reach.

Recent findings suggest that the fund is also looking at AI infrastructure such as data centres and chips. Kazah pointed to the region’s energy, land and closeness to the US. Power shortages, though, have held back data centres in Mexico.

Sources indicate that brazil and Mexico will stay its biggest markets, with Argentina and Colombia on the rise. Kaszek was founded in 2011 by former MercadoLibre executives Kazah and Nicolas Szekasy. Its portfolio includes digital bank Nubank, QuintoAndar and Kavak.

The raise stands out in a weak market. PitchBook ranks it the largest Latin America-focused venture fund to close since 2023. Only 14 venture funds closed in the region through September, it says, against 68 in all of 2023.

AI startups can still draw substantial cheques, though. In August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI wealth adviser built by former Nubank staff, raised an $85M seed round.
